items.title: Burnham pledges early intervention and ‘benefits backstop’ to tackle youth jobs crisis
items.summary:
Prime minister promises ‘root-and-branch rethink’ of support for young people as Milburn report advises sweeping changes to some benefits

Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”.

Burnham said the government would intervene at all the stages of life in which young people fell behind, and “long before they find themselves out of work and reliant on the state”, including providing more opportunities for vocational training in schools.

items.title: The crisis facing Britain’s young people is politicians’ fault. To fix it, we need a generational response | Andy Burnham
items.summary:
Alan Milburn’s review will mark a watershed moment for our approach to welfare and childhood. This is how I’m determined to create change

  • Report: Burnham pledges early intervention and ‘benefits backstop’ to tackle youth jobs crisis

A generation of young people did not wake up one morning and decide they did not want to work. The fact that a million 16- to 24-year-olds are now not in education, employment or training (Neet) is not their fault. It is ours, as politicians.

We have failed to give them the support they need as they have grown up in a tougher world. This has become an economic catastrophe for the country – and a moral one too.

Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United Kingdom

Continue reading...
items.t: The crisis facing Britain’s young people is politicians’ fault. To fix it, we need a generational response | Andy Burnham

items.title: FBI raids and a recycling firm: how a promising US mayor wound up at the center of a bribery scandal
items.summary:
As Oakland residents watch ex-mayor Sheng Thao stand trial, the scandal has come to symbolise wider frustrations

Two years ago, residents of Oakland, California, woke up to a shocking scene: their mayor’s home was being raided by the FBI. Agents were seen carrying dozens of boxes from the hilltop home of Sheng Thao, the city’s 38-year-old leader, as part of an investigation constituents would later learn alleged her participation in a pay-to-play scheme with the city’s recycling contractor.

It was a stunning moment for Thao, who was elected to lead the Bay Area city in 2022 and was once seen as a promising young mayor in a city that has long grappled with economic inequality and a reputation for violent crime. Her story of growing up in a refugee family and overcoming domestic violence and homelessness to become the first person of Hmong descent to run a major US city resonated with readers confronting questions about equity and representation that came to the fore during the Covid-19 pandemic, and made her the subject of glowing media profiles.

items.t: FBI raids and a recycling firm: how a promising US mayor wound up at the center of a bribery scandal

items.title: The ultimate adulting task: signing up for health insurance
items.summary:
Not many 22-year-olds share DJ Mikunda’s enthusiasm for health insurance coverage.

“You know what sounds like a good Friday night? It’s looking at health insurance,” he joked.

But Mikunda has a reason to be eager. He has gone without coverage since he left home and started working in 2023. He’s now a manager at a gas station in St. Louis.

In years past, he has looked at plans on the health insurance marketplace at healthcare.gov — but the options proved overwhelming and a bit too expensive.

“I feel like I’m a well-informed individual,” Mikunda said. “I try to stay updated on what a deductible is and what the premiums are and copays. And I’m still finding myself a little bit lost.”

To sort through the basics, HealthQ introduced Mikunda to independent assister Jackie Shrago , who has been helping people navigate the insurance marketplace since the early days of the Affordable Care Act.

The QTip: 

Search for a free “independent assister” on healthcare.gov to better understand your insurance options.

Income Drives the Conversation 

Shrago started by asking Mikunda about his income. How much money you expect to make in the coming year determines whether you’re eligible for reduced monthly payments. The system uses a sliding scale for households making less than 400% of the federal poverty rate — which means, for 2027 enrollees, an individual with no children can make up to $63,480 and still qualify for a discount.

A person in their mid-20s making $50,000, for instance, would get an average 23% discount, according to KFF’s subsidy calculator . For someone making…
items.t: The ultimate adulting task: signing up for health insurance

items.title: Gen Z believes using AI is making their colleagues dumb and lazy—but may paradoxically see it as key to their own promotion, Wharton says
items.summary:
Last year, researchers from Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon University revealed startling evidence about the impact of using AI on how—and how hard—people think, finding that among more than 300 knowledge workers, leaning too much on AI tools like ChatGPT was associated with diminished critical thinking skills .

The study, mirrored by results from MIT-led research , suggested that even using AI for low-stakes tasks such as proofreading “can lead to significant negative outcomes in high-stakes contexts,” like writing legal documents, the study authors wrote.

For the young generation of digital natives navigating AI anxiety around keeping up with peers using the technology and AI displacing them from jobs, the fear of the technology making people dumber is dominant. But that hasn’t stopped them from using AI—even when they’re explicitly told not to.

A Wharton-led survey published earlier this year, conducted in partnership with Gallup and the Walton Family Foundation, found young people are ramping up their AI use, even as their concerns about it causing lazy thinking persist. A survey of nearly 2,500 U.S. adults between the ages of 18 and 28 completed in October 2025 found 79% of respondents believed AI makes people lazier, and 62% said they had concerns it makes people less smart.

“What we find is deep ambivalence on how Gen Z is thinking [about] using AI,” Benjamin Lira Luttges, a postdoctoral scholar at Wharton who led research for the report, told Fortune .

Despite these fears, Gen Zers have increased their AI usage. Pew Research Center data published in June found…
items.t: Gen Z believes using AI is making their colleagues dumb and lazy—but may paradoxically see it as key to their own promotion, Wharton says

items.title: Barack Obama says work-life balance isn’t real for successful people
items.summary:
Former President Barack Obama admits that if you want to find career success , you shouldn’t expect to always have work–life balance; it’s okay to “throw yourself into work,” as long as you make up for it later, he says. After a hard-core campaign season, he set a strict rule as president to have dinner every night with Michelle and his two daughters, Sasha and Malia. 

If finding success in your career is on your bucket list, you might need to get used to working lunches and staying past 5 p.m. That’s, at least, according to former President Barack Obama , who revealed that achieving proper work–life balance will not always be possible. 

“If you want to be excellent at anything—sports, music, business, politics—there’s going to be times of your life when you’re out of balance, where you’re just working and you’re single-minded,” he admitted on The Pivot Podcast in 2024.

It’s a lesson he—and his family—learned the hard way. 

The 65-year-old said when he first ran for president, he was on the constant grind for over a year and a half. While he said he would take some breaks during the weekends, his wife, Michelle, was largely left picking up the slack at home, like taking care of the kids, even while she had a full-time job of her own.

Though the time away from his family led to two terms in the White House , Obama admitted it wasn’t sustainable. As president, he set a rule where he had family dinner every night at 6:30 p.m.—even if he had to go back to work later. And while some leaders might think it takes away valuable work time, he said the opportunity to decompress…
items.t: Barack Obama says work-life balance isn’t real for successful people

items.title: Gen Z’s job crisis has reached the ultrarich. Wealth advisors say billionaire parents are now planning for kids who may struggle to land and keep jobs
items.summary:
Even the wealthiest parents in America are worried about their kids’ financial futures. The unemployment rate for recent college graduates has held at about 5.6% , and 42.5% of recent grads were underemployed at the end of 2025, the highest share since 2020. A college degree no longer guarantees a steady paycheck , and economists warn AI could upend the entry-level work that recent grads have historically done.

In a world where seemingly no one is immune to the impacts of AI on the workforce and an increasingly stiff job market, ultra-high net worth people are starting to have the same concerns as middle-class and low-income families: Will my kid be able to get a job and support themself?

“Billionaires have the financial resources to support their children, but they sometimes struggle to determine what else is needed for their children to succeed,” Tom Thiegs, managing director of leadership and legacy at Ascent Private Capital Management with U.S. Bank, told Fortune earlier this year.

Millionaires and billionaires “are recognizing this is not the same game they had to play,” wealth manager Patrick Dwyer told CNBC earlier this year. “Families have to rethink … what it means to support their children. And we’re not talking about spoiling your kids. We’re talking about: What if your kid needs retraining at 33?” Dwyer is managing director at Aligned by NewEdge Wealth, a boutique wealth management firm based in Miami. He works with clients with net worths between roughly $100 million and more than $1 billion.

Dwyer said his clients are concerned their children, typically…
items.t: Gen Z’s job crisis has reached the ultrarich. Wealth advisors say billionaire parents are now planning for kids who may struggle to land and keep jobs

items.title: Skims’ $148 advent calendar flop wasn’t a stunt, marketers say—but store credit may not win back Kim Kardashian’s angry customers
items.summary:
“We might be on track for the worst advent calendar I’ve ever opened,” content creator Kayla Ryan said in a TikTok video this week, referring to the $148 Skims 12-day advent calendar that customers have been ripping apart for the past several days. 

“I could get these at Dollar Tree ,” she continued, pulling three unpacked hair ties from the day three slot on the advent calendar. The $148 box held keychains, bobby pins, scrunchies, and hair ties—but none of the bodysuits or loungewear that made Kim Kardashian’s company so popular.

Countless videos like Ryan’s have flooded social media for the past several days, prompting Skims to scramble to contain the fallout. In response to the online outrage, the company “personally contacted every customer who purchased the calendar and offered them a choice of a full refund or a SKIMS credit to put towards other products,” a spokesperson told other outlets. 

Skims did not respond to multiple requests for comment from Fortune .

The catch, according to the email buyers received, is that a cash refund means sending the calendar back, while shoppers who opt for store credit keep it. That detail led to some theories that Skims had purposefully rage-baited customers.

“Skims knew what they were doing with that advent calendar. I’d bet money it was intentional,” Jessica Tillery, a senior vice president of brand communications for Allison Worldwide, wrote in a LinkedIn post this week.

“Every dollar spent over that $148 credit is new revenue for them,” Tillery wrote. “Every person who comes back to shop with that credit is a repeat…
items.t: Skims’ $148 advent calendar flop wasn’t a stunt, marketers say—but store credit may not win back Kim Kardashian’s angry customers

items.title: Bodyguards aren’t enough: After Jensen Huang’s exit, CEOs need counterintelligence training
items.summary:
This month, Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia after acknowledging an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials suspect is a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia’s board said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” and China has denied the allegations.

A month earlier, OpenAI’s countermeasures team found a listening device in a San Francisco conference room where executives often held sensitive discussions. The FBI later arrested an OpenAI employee accused of planting it .

To most people, espionage belongs in spy thrillers. For C-suite executives, corporate espionage and executive targeting are a growing threat. Companies once seen as untouchable now face foreign espionage and physical targeting.

The problem isn’t awareness or money. Today’s executives have to change how they live, travel, and interact with the people around them to prepare for adversaries.

Big tech companies already spend millions on executive security. Nvidia, No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500, spent nearly $4 million protecting Huang in fiscal 2026, according to Fortune ‘s analysis of company filings , up from $3.5 million in 2024 .

The December 2024 killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson on a Manhattan sidewalk reminded S&P 500 companies that security reaches well beyond cybersecurity. Since then, spending has climbed. About 38% of S&P 500 companies provided security perks to at least some executives in 2025, up from 28% in 2023, according to an early look at proxy filings by executive data firm Equilar .

AI companies are a…
items.t: Bodyguards aren’t enough: After Jensen Huang’s exit, CEOs need counterintelligence training

items.title: I helped grow a steel company from $750 million to $12 billion. CEOs should use AI before they grade employees on it
items.summary:
“Raise your hand if your executive team has mandated the use of AI.”

I was standing on stage at the annual Great Places to Work convention in Las Vegas, and every one of the 500 CHROs I was in front of put their hands up. These were all HR leaders in mid-market and enterprise companies.

“Now, keep your hands up if every single person on your executive team is using AI to make themselves more valuable.”

Almost every hand went down.

I ask this question at every speaking engagement, and I’ve seen a pattern–and a problem. Company leaders are mandating the use of AI. With that mandate, they’re expecting increases in the productivity of their workforce. But they’re not holding themselves to the same standard.

Executives often think that “leading AI” in their organizations means delegating the adoption and strategy of it to IT, a Chief AI Officer, or an outside consultant. That’s not delegation–that’s abdication.

CEOs and executive teams need to learn to use AI, and become AI-driven leaders, before they can build AI-driven organizations.

I say this as I’m starting to see companies increasingly tying AI goals and skills directly to employee raises and promotions. Should compensation be tied to AI skill? It depends on the company. If you’re an organization that typically ties performance to specific skills that will grow in value, it makes sense. If you don’t, it’s a break from precedent–but it doesn’t mean it’s the wrong move.

What does concern me is when a CEO who doesn’t use AI is the one making the call. And by “use AI,” I don’t mean to help them write better emails–I…
items.t: I helped grow a steel company from $750 million to $12 billion. CEOs should use AI before they grade employees on it

items.title: ‘We are losing ground’: Professors log 55-hour weeks as pay stagnates and states question their workloads
items.summary:
Public universities helped make American higher education a draw for students and researchers worldwide. Now lawmakers and governing boards from Kansas to Utah want proof that the professors who teach there work hard enough.

Faculty say the premise is backward. Professors who spoke with Fortune describe 55-hour weeks, departments that have shrunk by as much as half, and raises that haven’t kept pace with inflation.

“We are losing ground,” said Renita Coleman , a journalism professor at the University of Texas at Austin.

As scrutiny of higher education grows , state legislators, governing boards, and administrators have started questioning how professors spend their time and whether they deliver enough for their salaries and job protections. Some have pushed to limit tenure . Others are demanding a detailed accounting of faculty responsibilities.

Critics see tenure as a shield for underperformers. Faculty say that misreads the job 

Public confidence in American higher education has fallen sharply over the past decade. According to Gallup , 38% of Americans expressed a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in higher education in 2026, down from 57% in 2015. The share expressing very little or no confidence rose from 10% to 25%.

The weakening trust comes amid a convergence of concerns, from rising college costs and questions about the value of degrees to political battles on campuses . Those frustrations have fueled skepticism of tenure, which grants professors permanent faculty status after they meet a university’s standards for teaching, research, and service.…
items.t: ‘We are losing ground’: Professors log 55-hour weeks as pay stagnates and states question their workloads

items.title: Is Burnham’s plan for a housing revolution anything more than a pipedream? | John Harris
items.summary:
Nearly 2 million children are housed in dire conditions, anxious families are living out of carrier bags. There’s little sign of the hope our PM promised

Two days after the Christmas of 2024, Andy Burnham put up a post on X that linked to a piece about housing in the Guardian. The then mayor of Greater Manchester, who was beginning to find his voice as a frank critic of Keir Starmer’s new government, did not mess about: “The Government should make building hundreds of thousands of council homes its defining purpose,” he said. “No other policy, achievable within a parliament, would have greater social and economic benefits.”

In his first Labour conference speech as party leader and prime minister, Burnham reprised much the same argument, promising “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar era”. But by that point, he had also served notice that his commitment to a thoroughgoing council house revival might not be quite as cast iron as it seemed. The previous month, having insisted that all of the £39bn Rachel Reeves had promised to spend on the Starmer government’s Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) until 2036 should go on homes for social rent, he made something of a brazen U-turn, announcing that the allocation of the first £10bn would reflect the existing social…

items.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
items.summary:
The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype

It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat.

The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness.
items.t: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI

items.title: Son of ex-Alamo Rent a Car owner went from hip hop label founder to lithium leader. He’s even eyeing the White House
items.summary:
An Elon Musk acolyte, Tesla driver, and serial entrepreneur, Teague Egan was imagining ways of breaking into renewable energy in 2018 while he took a vacation to Bolivia. He learned about the country’s salt flats, their lithium reserves potential and, eventually, about the industry’s antiquated lithium mining techniques.

“As an entrepreneur, I knew there had to be a better way. That was my ‘aha’ moment,” said Egan, now 38. He really began to think about how the lithium-ion batteries in Tesla’s electric vehicles are made and their massive global growth potential.

He quickly founded EnergyX—short for Energy Exploration Technologies—and this year became the only company mining lithium commercially in the U.S. with modern direct lithium extraction (DLE) technology at its new Project Lonestar site in East Texas . This summer, EnergyX also opened a project in Chile extracting 170 metric tons of lithium a year.

But these are still just demonstration plants. The real growth is about to begin, he touted.

“EnergyX is just going to keep our head down and move towards commercialization,” Egan told Fortune .

The plan is to commence construction next year. EnergyX aims to bring its Black Giant lithium project in Chile online by the end of 2028 with a first phase producing 7,500 tons per year and expanding to 52,500 tons annually by 2030. Project Lonestar in Texas would quickly follow with a 15,000-ton facility in 2029 and growing to 50,000 tons by 2031.

These are admittedly aggressive timelines, but Egan is confident the progress will pick up quickly after achieving a watershed…
items.t: Son of ex-Alamo Rent a Car owner went from hip hop label founder to lithium leader. He’s even eyeing the White House

items.title: AFC Wimbledon, a failed £87m investment bid and the challenge for fan ownership
items.summary:
Clubs with wealthy proprietors can maintain a loss-making operation but things can be more complex when the supporters carry the can

When you walk up from Haydons Road train station to Plough Lane there is a blue AFC Wimbledon billboard that reads “Fan owned football”, directly opposite the site of the old Plough Lane stadium where there are now blocks of flats. There is a memorial to the old Wimbledon FC – a reminder that supporters can often have little say in the running of their club – on the same corner, just up the road from the new Cherry Red Records Stadium.

AFC Wimbledon are one of only two majority fan-owned clubs in the EFL – along with Exeter City – but that makes running a loss-making operation, as 94% of teams in England’s top five tiers are doing according to the State of the Game report, even more challenging. “In other clubs, the owner just puts their hand in their pocket, produces cash,” said Hannah Kitcher, who has been a member of the Dons Trust Board (DTB), which runs AFC Wimbledon, for seven years. “It’s harder when the owners are fans – you can only go to them so many times.”

items.t: AFC Wimbledon, a failed £87m investment bid and the challenge for fan ownership

items.title: Gymshark in trademark battle that threatens future of small fitness business

items.title: ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick
items.summary:
Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true

The resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs involving one of the world’s most powerful men. As investigations mount into what went wrong at the $4tn chip company, the saga may also become a milestone in the decades-long history of spies infiltrating the US tech industry.

Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend, following a report from the New York Times that the tech mogul had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China’s government. Huang resigned on Thursday after 33 years as CEO amid reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees, causing the world’s most valuable chip company’s stock to plummet.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick

items.title: Italy fines Meta $887m for accessing Android users’ photos and videos
items.summary:
The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has imposed on a tech giant and Meta says it plans to appeal the decision

Italy’s data protection agency has fined Facebook parent company Meta €805m ($887m) for accessing users’ photos without their specific consent.

Through the Facebook application for Android devices, Meta accessed photographs, videos and related metadata belonging to Italian users “without obtaining specific consent and without properly informing them”, the authority said in a statement.

items.title: A rapid interest rate rise seems inevitable – and households are expected to pick up the tab
items.summary:
Raising borrowing costs too far risks laying waste to whatever growth there is in the economy

A head of steam is building up behind the Bank of England raising interest rates again. With the latest forecasts by the central bank showing inflation rising to 5% next spring, another increase in the cost of borrowing seems inevitable, and may come as soon as next month.

A growing number of analysts predict the Bank’s policymakers will don Scrooge masks when they meet on 17 December to deliver a message of austerity and sacrifice.

items.title: Interest rate rises likely in coming months, Bank of England’s chief economist says
items.summary:
‘We have further to go,’ says Huw Pill after increase to 4% this month as Bank seeks to tackle rising inflation

The Bank of England will probably need to raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027 to combat rising inflation, its chief economist has said.

Signalling a sharp rise in mortgage payments for an estimated 2.3 million homeowners who will have to refinance their loans next year, Huw Pill said that while the decision to nudge interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month was a “significant step” towards getting monetary policy into a better place, “we ⁠have further to go”.

Continue reading...
items.t: Interest rate rises likely in coming months, Bank of England’s chief economist says

items.title: Health is wealth? Polymarket and Kalshi now host bets on measles and other US health crises
items.summary:
Experts warn of risks of platforms hosting bets tied to US public health – including vaccine mandates and drug trials

The sign was pasted on a construction fence next to an elementary school in the Brooklyn borough of New York City. “Vaccines,” it proclaimed in bold capital letters against a blue star-spangled background – appearing, at first glance, to be like any other public health message on the importance of getting vaccinated.

But at the bottom of the sign, in smaller letters, it read: “Will any state end vaccine markets?” It was accompanied by the logo for Polymarket, an online prediction market where users can log in to wager on the outcomes of nearly any event – including, now, public health.

Continue reading...

items.title: Jensen Huang has a ‘rockstar’ reputation in Taiwan. Will it survive now that he’s out of Nvidia?
items.summary:
In Taiwan, Jensen Huang is more than a CEO. The Tainan-born Nvidia founder is a frequent visitor who dines with the island’s tech elite and draws fans wherever he goes. 

On Thursday, Huang resigned from the top job at Nvidia after reports of two extramarital affairs, one with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly believe is a Chinese intelligence asset.

Few places have more riding on Huang’s reputation than Taiwan, where TSMC , Foxconn and other suppliers form the backbone of Nvidia’s business and Huang is treated as a homegrown hero. Analysts there say Taiwanese are likely to forgive his personal failings. The allegations that Chinese intelligence may have exploited his relationships are another matter on an island that sees Beijing’s spying on its tech industry as a long-running national security threat.

Huang’s reputation is now in ruins in the U.S. following revelations that he had an extramarital affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia is also dogged by accusations that it facilitated Chinese access to its AI chips, which are subject to U.S. export controls. 

Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company , is now under scrutiny following a flurry of media reports about Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. Several media reports allege that Megaspeed helped Chinese companies get access to Nvidia AI processors, potentially in violation of U.S. export controls. (Beijing denies Alice Huang is a spy; Megaspeed has also denied allegations that…
items.t: Jensen Huang has a ‘rockstar’ reputation in Taiwan. Will it survive now that he’s out of Nvidia?
